issues.description: Non-descending wheels are a qualitatively different outcome from successfully descending wheels, yet they were recoded as exact zero-speed observations and analyzed in the same linear model. This creates a point mass at zero, mixes failure and performance processes, and makes Gaussian linear modeling of speed inappropriate. A two-part/hurdle model or separate analysis of failure probability and speed among successful descents would be more defensible.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. We fitted a linear model with "Speed" as the outcome variable

issues.description: The understanding outcome is a bounded discrete count based on 10 test items, but it was modeled with a linear model as if continuous and approximately Gaussian. This is a distributional mismatch; a binomial/item-level mixed model would better reflect the data-generating process and the bounded 0–10 scale.
issues.quote:
The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

We fitted a linear model with "Score" as the outcome variable

issues.description: The preregistered model distinguished inertia and centre-of-mass understanding, but after examining the data and encountering nonconvergence, the authors switched to an aggregated score. Because the two components were negatively correlated, aggregation can cancel domain-specific effects and bias the analysis toward a null conclusion about overall understanding.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia (Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: The content of inherited theories was not experimentally assigned. Participants in the theory condition inherited both the previous participant’s last two configurations/scores and whatever theory that participant happened to write. Therefore differences attributed to 'inheriting an inertia theory' or 'centre-of-mass theory' are confounded with inherited wheel examples, prior performance, and chain history, so causal claims about theory content are not identified.
issues.quote:
In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

All participants except those in the first generation were provided with social information. In the “Configurations” treatment (n = 70), the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in the chain were provided to the next participant in the chain. In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.description: The proposed mechanism that theory transmission canalizes exploration and thereby shapes understanding is inferred from post hoc associations, not from an experimental manipulation of exploration. Grouping participants after the fact by the wheels they produced does not permit causal inference about whether exploration caused understanding differences or merely correlated with them.
issues.quote:
To test this mechanism, we grouped participants who did not inherit any theory (i.e. from the “Configurations” treatment) into 3 categories: those who produced various types of wheels, those who only produced balanced wheels, and those who only produced unbalanced wheels.

These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.description: The paper equates a 10-item pairwise prediction task with 'causal understanding of the system.' That operationalization captures a narrow form of explicit comparative judgment about two preselected dimensions, not the broader construct invoked in the title and abstract. The authors' own discussion that participants had 'appropriate intuitions' further suggests the measure may miss tacit or partial causal knowledge that could support optimization.
issues.quote:
Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to predict which wheel would reach the bottom of the rails first.

It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space.

This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration

issues.description: The core manipulation of 'theory transmission' was a very short text string with a forced sentence stem. This impoverished format may be a poor proxy for transmitting a causal model and could substantially attenuate any true benefit of richer explanation, instruction, demonstration, or dialogue. A null effect of this manipulation cannot be straightforwardly generalized to 'causal model transmission' broadly.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.description: The experimenter manually implemented participants’ chosen configurations on the physical wheel, yet data collection was not blinded to condition. This creates avoidable risk of expectancy effects or subtle implementation bias in apparatus setup, release, or interaction with participants.
issues.quote:
Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly

Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: No a priori sample-size justification was provided, even though the effective independent units are chains, not individual participants. With only 14 chains per treatment, the study may be underpowered for treatment comparisons, making null claims especially difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Two treatments were run. In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females). No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.description: The manuscript states that Bayesian multilevel models were fit, but it does not report the priors used. Priors are essential for evaluating, reproducing, and interpreting Bayesian analyses, especially with relatively small chain-level samples and convergence problems.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32.  Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: The manuscript never explains how the 10-item understanding score was computed, whether any item had 'No difference' as the correct answer, or what exact chance level corresponds to the 'random guesser' reference. Without the scoring key and rule, the central understanding measure cannot be fully evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote:
For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.description: The manuscript describes the timed interval as 92 cm between switches, but elsewhere says speed was calculated as 1 m divided by descent time. If timing was actually over 92 cm, the reported speeds are inflated by a constant factor, and payoff scaling/maximal-speed claims become unclear.
issues.quote:
The physical system was a wheel that traveled down a 1-meter long inclined track.

Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails

The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations

issues.description: For understanding, the reported Generation × Treatment interval does not include zero, yet the authors conclude that the analyses do not substantially support an effect of theory transmission. This is inconsistent with their interval-based inferential framing and obscures the evidential status of the interaction.
issues.quote: Treatment 95% CI: (-2.54, 0.31), mean = -1.14; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen’s kappa for coding performed by five raters. Cohen’s kappa is defined for two raters; with five raters, a multi-rater statistic (e.g., Fleiss’ kappa) or a clearly described average of pairwise kappas should be reported. As written, the reliability statistic is inappropriate or incompletely specified.
issues.quote:
5 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel (i.e. the respective role of inertia and centre of mass in the performance of the wheel) and were asked to code participants’ theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass.

Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.description: Key mechanistic claims are based on explicitly exploratory analyses with very small subgroups and post hoc recategorizations. In particular, the 'full theory' subgroup has only 6 participants, making descriptive heat maps and downstream interpretations unstable and highly sensitive to idiosyncratic cases.
issues.quote:
Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior (Supplementary Figure 1).

Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the “Configurations + Theory” treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

The few participants who inherited a full theory produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (Figure 3D and H).

issues.description: All participants saw the same 10 test items in the same order. Without counterbalancing or randomization, item difficulty is confounded with order effects such as practice, fatigue, and cueing. This is especially problematic because theories were elicited immediately after the test, so the fixed order may also have shaped the transmitted explanations.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: The study uses French university students optimizing a highly constrained, low-dimensional apparatus with immediate quantitative feedback over just five trials. Extending these findings to 'complex technologies,' archaeological inference, or human expansion is much broader than the design supports. Real technologies are typically higher-dimensional, socially embedded, and often provide delayed/noisy feedback.
issues.quote:
These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

Finally, although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional

issues.description: Participants generated the theory to be transmitted only after completing the understanding test. The test itself explicitly focused attention on the causal dimensions later coded in the theories, so the manipulation does not reflect purely spontaneous theory generation from task experience alone.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to write their theory after the test phase was completed.

issues.description: The main Bayesian model for treatment differences in speed had poor sampling efficiency and low effective sample size for at least one parameter. Although the authors refer to additional models in the supplement, the main text does not provide enough detail for readers to evaluate how serious the problem was or whether conclusions are robust to specification choices.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3). The robustness of the model estimates was checked by running additional models (see below). Additional models with more efficient sampling confirmed the reported results (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 and Supplementary Figure 8).

issues.description: The authors explicitly state that analyses were not performed blind to condition. In a study with post hoc analytic changes and exploratory subgrouping, unblinded analysis increases the risk of researcher degrees of freedom and confirmation bias affecting modeling and interpretation.
issues.quote: Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: The abstract claims theory transmission had 'no noticeable effect' on cultural evolution, but the reported treatment intervals are wide and compatible with both meaningful benefits and harms. This is an overstatement of what the data support: imprecise estimates do not justify a strong null conclusion.
issues.quote:
Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

Results show that the average wheel speed increased at a similar rate in the "Configurations + Theory" as it did in the "Configurations" treatment (Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h, Figure 2.A)
